content: The text provided is a long and detailed list of references, guidelines, and professional affiliations related to nutrition, dietary guidelines, and public health. It includes citations of systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and WHO guidelines on topics such as potassium intake, carbohydrate quality, fruit and vegetable consumption, legume consumption, saturated and trans-fatty acids, and their associations with health outcomes like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and mortality. Additionally, it lists members of various expert groups, their areas of expertise, and their contributions to the development of dietary guidelines. 1. The WHO has published guidelines on potassium intake for adults and children, emphasizing its importance in maintaining cardiovascular health and reducing the risk of hypertension. These guidelines are accessible through the WHO IRIS platform. 2. The WHO has also issued recommendations on carbohydrate intake for adults and children, focusing on the quality of carbohydrates and their role in preventing chronic diseases. This document is available on the WHO publications website. 3. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Reynolds et al. (2019) in The Lancet examined the quality of carbohydrates and their impact on human health, highlighting the benefits of high-quality carbohydrates in reducing the risk of chronic diseases. 4. Aune et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Epidemiology, which demonstrated that higher fruit and vegetable intake is associated with a reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all-cause mortality. 5. Marventano et al. (2017) reviewed the relationship between legume consumption and cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in Public Health Nutrition, concluding that legumes are beneficial for heart health. 6. Afshin et al. (2014) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, showing that nut and legume consumption is linked to a lower risk of ischemic heart disease, stroke, and diabetes. 7. Mytton et al. (2017) published an erratum in BMC Public Health regarding their systematic review and meta-analysis on the effects of increased fruit and vegetable consumption on body weight and energy intake. 8. Zong et al. (2016) investigated the intake of individual saturated fatty acids and their association with coronary heart disease risk in two large U.S. cohort studies, published in BMJ. Their findings suggest that specific saturated fatty acids may have varying effects on heart health. 9. Downs et al. (2013) reviewed the effectiveness of policies aimed at reducing dietary trans fats in Bulletin of the World Health Organization, emphasizing the importance of regulatory measures in improving public health. 10. L’Abbé et al. (2009) discussed strategies for eliminating trans fats from the food supply in both industrialized and developing countries in European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 11. The WHO has released guidelines on saturated and trans-fatty acid intake for adults and children, aiming to reduce the global burden of non-communicable diseases. 12. The Global Nutrition Policy Review 2016–2017 assessed country-level progress in creating policy environments that promote healthy diets and nutrition. 13. Griffin et al. (2021) explored the variability in serum LDL-cholesterol response to dietary fatty acids in Atherosclerosis, addressing controversies surrounding fat quality and cardiovascular disease risk. 14. Annexes in the document list members of the WHO steering group and guideline development group, detailing their areas of expertise, such as human nutrition, epidemiology, public health, and systematic review methodologies. 15. The document also includes declarations of interest for members involved in the guideline development process, ensuring transparency and addressing potential conflicts of interest.
